setter.evidence: No setter named anywhere. The rep references an inbound application — 'I already saw your application' — and an earlier contact where he learned the prospect's wife had car trouble, but no setter appears in the title or the transcript. Notably no price pre-framing had been done, which is the central fact of this call.

prospect.name: Richard Kellis
prospect.occupation: Former professional musician, former lifeguard and retired high school music teacher (30 years directing bands and orchestras). Now employed in an unnamed role with a boss, working 40-50 hours a week, recently 50-70 while covering his fired boss's job; Mondays and Tuesdays are meant to be days off. Occupation was never asked.
prospect.family_status: Married. Two daughters aged 24 and two grandsons. House due to be paid off in about a year. Family longevity is pronounced — father lived to 95, great-grandfather to 99, aunts and uncles into their 90s.
prospect.training_background: Lifelong athlete — basketball, water polo, and a lifeguard who set the Huntington Beach two-mile run record. Pre-pandemic was swimming a mile four times a week and running four miles. Now walks 10,000-20,000 steps a day including three-to-five-mile hikes, kayaked two or three times a week until the last six months, and is a YMCA member where he swims. Tried a prescribed YMCA weights circuit and abandoned it — 'there was no joy'. Peaked at 230 lb; got down to 170 pre-pandemic on a juice cleanse plus elimination diet.
prospect.medical: Two shoulder surgeries over ten years ago on the right shoulder — torn labrum and torn rotator cuff — attributed to 30 years of conducting. Knee injury roughly 50 years ago with torn ligaments and a bone chip, recovered. Balance problems: stumbled on a walk three weeks before the call and scraped his arm and knee. Almost no flexibility, very tight hamstrings. Gluten intolerance, not celiac, self-diagnosed via an elimination protocol. Was hit hard by his first COVID infection with breathing issues and says he never fully recovered physically since, though the breathing issues have resolved.

signals: Lost ground to a specific hard season and names it: 'I did that until pandemic hit and pandemic just knocked me out. I got COVID and it hit me really hard... I just never really recovered physically since then'
Wants a former self back with a precise number attached — 160 lb, the weight he held at the end of his 40s, and in a dream scenario the 135 lb he carried at 40
Visible regret about the gap between self-image and reality: 'I've never been an excuse maker' followed by 'I realized that I'm just making excuses not to get started'

The waddle-versus-run line is the whole avatar in one sentence: 'you see the light at the end of the tunnel... and I realized that the light's there, but I'm going to waddle through it instead of run through it. And that's not the way I want to be'

Overlaps materially with skeptical_bargain_hunter: he is self-directed, has free YMCA access and a free nutritionist, and holds a diet protocol that demonstrably took him to 170 lb before. What separates him is that he was not sceptical of the method — he was thirty times outside the price

goals.text: Get down to 160 lb from 210 — about 50 lb — and in an ideal world nearer 135 with a six-pack, which he treats as a byproduct rather than the aim
Get back to swimming a mile three or four times a week and kayaking four or five miles regularly
Run a full marathon, a lifelong ambition prompted by a niece who completed one
Fix the balance problems — he stumbled and fell on a walk three weeks earlier and would have caught himself in his youth
Regain flexibility, which he discovered he had almost none of when he tried his sister's yoga class
Be fit enough next year, when the house is paid off, to choose between buying a farm and travelling — 'if I tire too easily, if I'm carrying too much weight, then I won't be able to travel'
Live past 100 and not spend 30 years overweight — his family routinely reaches their 90s and he has wanted to be the first past 100 since he was six
Be a better parent to his 24-year-old daughters and be part of his two grandsons' lives
Wiry functional strength rather than size — 'I don't want to have a pair of guns' — enough for archery and slingshot
Find something he actually enjoys, because he only sustains what brings him joy

pains.text: 100 lb heavier than his high school weight and 50 lb above his target; peaked at 230
Weight affecting everything, starting with needing more sleep — 'my weight seems to affect all of my life'
Balance failure severe enough to cause a fall three weeks earlier
Almost no flexibility and very tight hamstrings
Never physically recovered from a severe first COVID infection with breathing complications
Six months of 50-70 hour weeks covering a fired boss's job on top of his own, leaving no energy for anything else
Chronic excuse-making he recognises and dislikes in himself — 'I keep finding excuses not to start'
Prescribed, impersonal exercise kills his motivation — the YMCA weights circuit 'was like working in the fast food industry... there was no joy'
Gluten intolerance his wife believes is psychosomatic, which he finds difficult
Carrying debts, with the house not paid off until next year

objections.raw_quote: That is a lot higher than I expected... So I don't know that I'll have 6,000 in discretionary funds for the next six months that I can throw in there.
objections.rep_response: Isolated it immediately and correctly — 'out of the finances, you feel like, yes, I want to do this, or not really?' — and got 'If I could afford it, yes, I would do this.' Then offered to have a conversation about finances.

objections.raw_quote: 6,000 is a very high price. I know a lot of people that would be able to afford that, but I've got debts and things, and there's no way I can afford 6,000.
objections.rep_response: Asked twice what range would be workable 'without putting no food on the table every month'. No financial picture was taken and no payment plan was offered, even after the prospect himself raised the subject.

objections.raw_quote: I mean, I can get a gym membership. Actually, I've got the YMCA. I can go work out at the YMCA for free. I won't have the guidance. I have an ex-student who's a nutritionist who has guided me off and on when I've had nutritional questions.
objections.rep_response: Never rebutted the substitute. Countered with differentiation instead — 'for 50 a month, you're never going to find something that's actually customized to you' — which answers a question the prospect had not asked.

objections.raw_quote: It's not that my health isn't worth $6,000. It's that there are other ways that I can do things that's not going to cost me $6,000 and I can get healthy... I don't need to spend $6,000 to validate that I need to do this. It's just a matter of doing it.
objections.rep_response: Held the price honestly rather than discounting — 'Trevor is definitely not the cheapest, I can tell you you're going to be able to find cheaper things, I'm sure' — and asked whether he wanted something genuinely customised or just to get started with something.

objections.raw_quote: in the very beginning, when I told my wife I was having this meeting, she's like, well, you know, you're not going to spend very much... obviously, I have to run it by her as well
objections.rep_response: Never addressed. By this point the price gap had already decided the call.

evidence: Explicit and repeated no: 'at this point, I'm about ready to say, no, this isn't for me, period. I just don't see how this is going to work' and later 'at this point, I don't think this is for me'
The $3,000 tier was also refused: 'Yes, that's still out of my range'
The gap is structural, not negotiable — he expected 'any kind of a membership where it's 30, 40 a month'
The rep effectively disqualified him too: 'if you feel like, well, I'm looking to spend like maybe a hundred max, then I would say this is definitely not for you'
Counter-evidence: he wanted the outcome badly and said so — 'If I could afford it, yes, I would do this' — and 'It's not that my health isn't worth $6,000'
Counter-evidence: a genuinely warm ending, and he may return next year when the house is paid off and his position changes
outcome.next_step: None booked. Rep pointed him to Trevor's free YouTube channel and invited questions.

notable.note: A qualification failure, not a selling failure. This prospect arrived expecting a $30-40 per month membership and was quoted $6,000 — roughly a thirty-fold gap — and there is no setter named anywhere on this call and no evidence of any price pre-framing before it. Compare the Rudolph call the previous day, where Kim had already given the prospect 'an insight from what the costs are going to look like' and price landed calmly. Fifty-three minutes of good discovery were spent on someone who could never buy. Credit where due: once the gap appeared the rep behaved well — he refused to discount, told the prospect plainly that cheaper options exist and that Trevor is at the top of the market, and pointed him to the free YouTube content rather than pushing. Two further notes. He has two shoulder surgeries on his right side, a repaired labrum and rotator cuff, and asked directly whether kettlebells would even help his balance ('I really don't, in all honesty, I don't really know') — neither was ever properly answered. And the rep misnamed him twice, as 'Darren' at 00:00:20 and 'Richie' at 00:44:56, which is the third call in this batch with a name error.
